newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Ebner sees orders triggering Roche surge.
newsitem.headline: Ebner sees orders triggering Roche surge.

text.p: Swiss banker Martin Ebner said he suspected the sudden surge in the shares of Roche Holding AG this week was based on a few substantial orders from foreign investors and this had triggered additional purchases by banks that had issued uncovered warrants on the shares.

Ebner, on the board of investment group Pharma Vision 2000 AG, told reporters that last year's merger of Sandoz AG and Ciba-Geigy AG into Novartis AG had lead to large porfolio shifts into Sandoz and Ciba to the detriment of Roche.
At the middle of 1996 Pharma Vision, part of Ebner's BZ Group Holding, held 14.4 percent of Roche's bearer shares.

On their own Sandoz and Ciba had accounted for a total of around 16 percent of the make-up of the blue-chip Swiss Market Index (SMI). But following the merger, Novartis accounted for some 23 percent of SMI.
Investors that wanted to have SMI-weighted porfolios therefore had to buy additional Sandoz and Ciba shares and had likely financed this be selling Roche shares, Ebner said.
In addition, Roche had said that 1996 and 1997 were transition years with operating profits first really rising in 1998 and 1999 with the introduction of new products.
A third factor was the depreciation of the Swiss franc and the Swiss National Bank's (SNB) willingness to keep interest rates down, which would keep the franc weak.
Faced with these factors, foreign investors had sold Swiss shares, including Roche.

However, following Roche's announcement of its 1996 sales figures last week, some investors had taken a second look at their portfolios and realised just how attractive Roche is and decided to buy its stock.
These buy orders, which Ebner described as serious and by long-term investors, had pushed Roche's share price higher and taken some banks, with unhedged warrants on Roche, by surprise.
These banks then had to quickly cover their positions.

On Wednesday Roche's non-voting equity securities, its most liquid security, rose seven percent in very active trade, amidst a flurry of rumours that Roche was to divest some of its activities and use the money to bid for another company.
Roche's 11 percent rise in 1996 sales to 15.96 billion Swiss francs had confirmed to analysts that Roche was on track to boost 1996 profits by 15 percent.
The day Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB), for example, forecast a 25 percent upside in Roche's stock over the next 18 to 24 months.
